title: Temple Cleansing
location: Jerusalem Temple, Court of the Gentiles
audience: Pilgrims, merchants, money changers, religious leaders
scholarly_note: The Temple Cleansing is reported in all four Gospels. John places it at the beginning of Jesus's ministry (John 2), while the Synoptics place it during Passion Week. Scholars debate whether there were two cleansings or one event placed differently for theological reasons. The Court of the Gentiles was the only place non-Jews could worship, but it had become a marketplace. Jesus's action is a prophetic sign-act of judgment, echoing Jeremiah 7 and Malachi 3. The commercial activity was necessary (pilgrims needed unblemished animals and proper currency for temple tax), but exploitation and corruption had turned sacred space into profit center.

old_testament.text: For my house will be called a house of prayer for all nations
old_testament.parallel: Matthew 21:13 'My house shall be called a house of prayer'
old_testament.significance: Jesus quotes Isaiah's vision of temple as place of worship for all nations. The Court of the Gentiles, meant for non-Jewish worship, had become commercial space. Jesus's cleansing reclaims space for Gentile prayer, foreshadowing Gospel's extension to all nations.

old_testament.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?
old_testament.parallel: Matthew 21:13 'you have made it a den of robbers'
old_testament.significance: Jeremiah 7 context: false security in temple while practicing injustice. A 'den of robbers' is not a place where robbery occurs but a hideout where robbers retreat after crimes. Jesus accuses leaders of using temple as refuge while exploiting people. Jeremiah 7 prophesied temple's destruction; Jesus's action foreshadows same judgment (fulfilled 70 CE).

old_testament.text: Zeal for your house consumes me, and the insults of those who insult you have fallen on me
old_testament.significance: Psalm 69 is messianic suffering psalm quoted multiple times in NT. Jesus's zeal for God's house leads to his suffering and death. His cleansing provokes authorities' final determination to kill him (Mark 11:18).

old_testament.text: The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple... He will sit as a refiner and purifier... he will purify the sons of Levi
old_testament.parallel: Jesus's sudden arrival and purifying action
old_testament.significance: Malachi prophesied Messiah would come suddenly to temple to purify worship. Jesus's cleansing fulfills this, judging corrupt temple system and foreshadowing new worship 'in spirit and truth' (John 4:23-24).

old_testament.text: From the lips of children and infants you have ordained praise because of your enemies, to silence the foe and the avenger
old_testament.parallel: Matthew 21:16 Jesus quotes to chief priests
old_testament.significance: Jesus defends children's praise by citing Psalm 8. While religious leaders reject him, children recognize truth. This echoes Matthew 11:25—God reveals truth to 'little children' while hiding it from 'wise and learned.' Children's praise fulfills Scripture; leaders' rejection condemns them.

historical_context.parallel: Annas family control of temple market
historical_context.significance: High priest Annas (father-in-law of Caiaphas) and his family controlled temple commerce, creating monopoly that exploited pilgrims. The 'Bazaar of Annas' on Mount of Olives sold sacrificial animals at inflated prices. Jesus's action directly challenged this economic exploitation controlled by high priestly family.

historical_context.parallel: Temple tax and currency exchange requirements
historical_context.significance: Every Jewish male paid annual half-shekel temple tax using Tyrian silver (purest silver available, despite pagan imagery). Money changers exchanged various currencies for temple-approved coins, charging fees. Animal sellers provided unblemished sacrifices. These services were necessary but had become exploitative.

Jesus's cleansing prophetically enacts coming judgment. In 70 CE, Romans destroyed temple, ending sacrificial system. Jesus's action and words ('destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it'—John 2:19) point to himself as replacement: the true temple where God dwells and people meet God.

rabbinic_parallels.text: Woe to me because of the house of Annas, woe to me because of their serpent's hiss!
rabbinic_parallels.parallel: Popular lament against high priestly corruption
rabbinic_parallels.significance: Later rabbinic tradition preserved memory of Annas family's corruption. The Talmud records popular woes against four high priestly families who abused power. Jesus's cleansing addressed widely recognized injustice, not merely religious scruples.

sections.title: Driving Out the Money Changers: 'Den of Robbers'
text: Jesus entered into the temple of God, and drove out all of those who sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers' tables and the seats of those who sold the doves. He said to them, 'It is written, "My house shall be called a house of prayer," but you have made it a den of robbers!'

controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: Hieron = temple complex; naos = inner sanctuary/Holy Place
controversial_terms.explanation: Greek has two temple words. 'Hieron' refers to the entire temple complex including courts; 'naos' refers specifically to the inner sanctuary building (Holy Place and Holy of Holies). Jesus cleansed the 'hieron'—specifically the Court of the Gentiles, outermost area. Only 'naos' was restricted to priests. Later (John 2:19-21), Jesus refers to his body as 'naos'—the true dwelling place of God.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: Jesus didn't violate sanctity of inner sanctuary reserved for priests. He acted in the public Court of the Gentiles, the only space where non-Jews could worship. Commercial activity in this court prevented Gentile worship, violating Isaiah 56:7's vision of 'house of prayer for all nations.' The location matters: Jesus reclaims space for Gentile inclusion.

controversial_terms.common_mistranslation: Greedy bankers doing something inherently wrong
controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: Currency exchangers for temple tax (necessary service that became exploitative)
controversial_terms.explanation: 'Kollybistēs' comes from 'kollybos' (small coin/exchange rate). These changers converted various currencies into Tyrian shekels required for temple tax. The service was necessary (pilgrims came from across empire with different currencies), but it had become exploitative, with inflated exchange rates enriching the Annas family who controlled the monopoly.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: Jesus isn't condemning necessary religious infrastructure but exploitation of pilgrims. Modern readers miss that temple tax required specific pure silver coins (Tyrian shekels). The issue isn't money in temple per se but corrupt priests using religious obligation to extract wealth from poor pilgrims. Jesus's anger targets injustice, not legitimate religious practice.

controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: House of prayer [for all nations—Isaiah 56:7 context]
controversial_terms.explanation: Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7, which reads 'My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations.' Matthew abbreviates, but the full quote (in Mark 11:17) includes 'for all nations.' The Court of the Gentiles was the only space where non-Jews could approach Israel's God. Turning it into noisy marketplace prevented Gentile worship.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: This isn't about prayer vs commerce generally but about Gentile exclusion specifically. Jesus's mission includes 'all nations' (Matt 28:19). The cleansing anticipates gospel's universal reach: barriers preventing Gentiles from worshiping God must be removed. This foreshadows temple's obsolescence—worship 'in spirit and truth' transcends location (John 4:21-24).

controversial_terms.common_mistranslation: Place where robbery happens / thieves' hideout
controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: Hideout of bandits (place robbers retreat to after committing crimes)
controversial_terms.explanation: The phrase quotes Jeremiah 7:11. A 'den' or cave is where robbers hide after robbery, not where robbery occurs. Jeremiah's point: people commit injustice all week, then retreat to temple for safety, treating it as sanctuary that rubber-stamps their sin. Jesus accuses leaders of similar hypocrisy: exploiting people through corrupt temple system while claiming religious legitimacy.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: Jesus isn't saying the temple has become a place of theft (like 'robbers' market') but a refuge for those who rob elsewhere. The leaders exploit pilgrims economically, then use temple piety as cover. This is systemic injustice hidden behind religious facade. Jeremiah's temple sermon (Jer 7) led to temple's destruction in 586 BCE; Jesus's action foreshadows 70 CE destruction.

controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: Drove out / Expelled forcefully / Cast out
controversial_terms.explanation: 'Ekballō' is a strong verb meaning to drive out, expel, or cast out. It's used for exorcism (driving out demons) and forceful removal. John 2:15 adds Jesus made a whip of cords. This isn't gentle persuasion but prophetic sign-act using force. Jesus physically overturns tables and drives animals and people out.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: This shatters 'gentle Jesus meek and mild' domestications. Jesus uses physical force in righteous anger against systemic injustice. This is zeal for God's house (Ps 69:9), not sinful anger. The action is prophetic theater—dramatic sign of coming judgment on corrupt temple system. Prophets often used symbolic acts (Ezekiel, Jeremiah); Jesus does the same.

scholarly_interpretation.summary: Jesus enters the temple complex and forcefully drives out merchants and money changers, overturning their tables. He quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, condemning the transformation of sacred space meant for prayer (especially Gentile prayer) into an exploitative marketplace. This prophetic sign-act enacts judgment on corrupt temple leadership and foreshadows temple's destruction.
key_points: Location is Court of the Gentiles—only place non-Jews could worship, now clogged with commerce
Commercial activity was necessary (pilgrims needed animals and proper currency) but had become exploitative monopoly controlled by high priestly family
Isaiah 56:7 quote emphasizes 'for all nations'—Jesus champions Gentile access to God
Jeremiah 7:11 reference evokes prophet's temple sermon predicting destruction—Jesus implies same judgment coming
This is prophetic sign-act, not impulsive anger. Prophets used dramatic symbolic actions to communicate God's message
The action directly challenges authority and economic interests of chief priests, accelerating plot to kill Jesus (Mark 11:18)

common_misinterpretations.error: Jesus opposes all money/commerce in religious contexts
common_misinterpretations.correction: The issue isn't money in temple per se but exploitation of worshipers and exclusion of Gentiles. Temple tax required currency exchange (Tyrian shekels mandated). Animal sales were necessary (pilgrims couldn't bring sacrifices from distant lands). Jesus condemns the corruption—inflated prices, monopolistic control by corrupt priests, and commercial activity preventing Gentile worship. The problem is injustice under religious cover, not religious infrastructure.
common_misinterpretations.scholars: E.P. Sanders notes temple commerce was necessary and legitimate. Craig Keener emphasizes the location (Court of Gentiles) as key—commerce there prevented Gentile worship. N.T. Wright frames this as prophetic enactment of judgment on corrupt leadership, not rejection of temple worship itself.

common_misinterpretations.error: Jesus's anger shows he sinned or lost control
common_misinterpretations.correction: Jesus's action is controlled, purposeful, prophetic theater—not impulsive rage. Righteous anger against injustice isn't sin (Eph 4:26 'be angry and do not sin'). Jesus quotes Scripture, making clear theological point. This is 'zeal for God's house' (Ps 69:9), not sinful loss of control. Prophets like Jeremiah performed dramatic acts (smashing jars, wearing yokes). Jesus's cleansing is prophetic sign-act communicating God's judgment on corruption.
common_misinterpretations.scholars: All major scholars recognize this as prophetic symbolism. The action is theatrical—overturning tables, driving out animals with whip—designed to shock and communicate message. William Barclay notes Jesus's anger is always against injustice toward others, never personal offense. This is holy anger, not sinful wrath.

common_misinterpretations.error: 'Den of robbers' means the temple marketplace was site of theft
common_misinterpretations.correction: A 'den' is where robbers hide after committing crimes elsewhere—not where they rob. Jeremiah 7:11's point: people sin all week, then treat temple as sanctuary that legitimizes their behavior. Jesus accuses temple leadership of exploiting people economically while hiding behind religious piety. The temple system itself has become tool of oppression, with religious authorities using it to extract wealth from poor pilgrims. They rob in the name of God, then retreat to temple's sanctity.
common_misinterpretations.scholars: Jeremiah 7 context is crucial. The prophet condemns trusting in temple's inviolability ('the temple of the LORD') while practicing injustice. God rejects worship disconnected from ethics. Jesus applies this: temple leadership uses religious system to exploit people, treating temple as legitimizing cover for corruption.

sections.title: Healing the Blind and Lame; Children's Praise
text: The blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children who were crying in the temple and saying, 'Hosanna to the son of David!' they were indignant, and said to him, 'Do you hear what these are saying?' Jesus said to them, 'Yes. Did you never read, "Out of the mouth of babes and nursing babies you have perfected praise"?'

controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: Blind and lame [specifically excluded from full temple participation—2 Samuel 5:8]
controversial_terms.explanation: 2 Samuel 5:8 records David's conquest of Jerusalem with cryptic reference to 'blind and lame' being hated. Rabbinic tradition interpreted this as excluding blind and lame from temple worship. Mishnah prohibits physically blemished from priestly service. By healing the blind and lame in the temple, Jesus overturns this exclusion, demonstrating the kingdom includes those religious law marginalized.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: Jesus's healing in temple directly challenges exclusionary purity laws. After cleansing temple of commercial corruption, he fills it with those considered ritually unacceptable. This illustrates the kingdom's values: religious system excluded the disabled; Jesus welcomes and heals them. The temple establishment witnessed him both challenging their economic exploitation and their purity boundaries.

controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: Wonderful/marvelous things [miraculous signs revealing God's power]
controversial_terms.explanation: 'Thaumasios' means marvelous, wonderful, astonishing—often with divine connotation. These aren't just impressive deeds but signs revealing God's presence and kingdom arrival. The healings validate Jesus's authority to cleanse temple and judge the system. Isaiah 35:5-6 prophesied in messianic age 'eyes of the blind will be opened, ears of the deaf unstopped, the lame will leap.' Jesus's healings fulfill this.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: The leaders witness messianic signs (cleansing, healing blind/lame, fulfilling Isaiah) but remain hardened. Their indignation at children's praise reveals spiritual blindness. They see the wonders but reject their significance. This fulfills Isaiah 6:9-10—seeing but not perceiving. The physically blind receive sight; the religious leaders remain spiritually blind.

controversial_terms.explanation: 'Hosanna' transliterates Hebrew 'hoshia na' (save now/please). It's from Psalm 118:25, part of Hallel psalms sung at Passover. Originally a prayer ('save us'), it became an acclamation ('salvation!'). By shouting 'Hosanna to Son of David,' children acclaim Jesus as Davidic Messiah who brings God's salvation. The leaders hear this as blasphemous messianic claim.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: The children aren't offering vague praise but making specific messianic claim—Jesus is Son of David who brings salvation. The leaders understand this perfectly, hence their indignation. That children, not religious experts, recognize truth fulfills Jesus's earlier saying: 'You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children' (Matt 11:25).

controversial_terms.english: out of the mouth of babes
controversial_terms.greek: ἐκ στόματος νηπίων καὶ θηλαζόντων (ek stomatos nēpiōn kai thēlazontōn)
controversial_terms.scholarly_translation: From the mouth of infants and nursing babies [God ordains praise from the unlikely]
controversial_terms.explanation: Jesus quotes Psalm 8:2 (LXX): 'Out of the mouth of babes and nursing infants you have perfected praise to silence the enemy and the avenger.' The psalm contrasts human frailty (infants) with cosmic enemies (foes, avengers). God uses weak things to shame the powerful. Children's praise fulfills Scripture, while educated leaders reject Messiah.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: This isn't sentimentality about children but divine reversal. God reveals truth to 'babes' while hiding it from 'wise' (Matt 11:25). The irony: chief priests demand Jesus silence children's messianic acclamation, but Scripture itself ordains it. The leaders, supposed Scripture experts, reveal they don't understand Scripture. Children's praise is more theologically accurate than priests' rejection.

controversial_terms.explanation: 'Aganakteō' means to be indignant, to feel strong displeasure or anger. This isn't mild irritation but deep offense. The leaders are outraged at children proclaiming Jesus as Messiah. They see this as blasphemy and loss of control—Jesus is allowing (even endorsing) messianic acclamation in the temple they control.
controversial_terms.why_it_matters: The leaders' indignation reveals their hardness. They witness miraculous healings (blind see, lame walk—Isaiah's messianic signs) and hear children praise God, yet they're angry instead of joyful. Their concern is control and authority, not truth. This contrasts sharply with children's open recognition of Jesus. The guardians of religious truth are most resistant to it.

scholarly_interpretation.summary: After cleansing the temple, Jesus heals the blind and lame within its courts—people traditionally excluded from full temple participation. Children acclaim him as 'Son of David' (messianic title). Religious leaders are indignant at the acclaim. Jesus defends the children by quoting Psalm 8:2, affirming God ordains praise from babes while learned leaders reject him.
key_points: Healing blind and lame fulfills Isaiah 35:5-6 (messianic signs) and reverses 2 Samuel 5:8's exclusion
Jesus transforms cleansed temple into place of healing and inclusion, not commercial exploitation and exclusion
Children's 'Hosanna to Son of David' is explicit messianic acclamation, not generic praise
Leaders understand the claim perfectly—hence indignation. They want Jesus to silence the 'blasphemy'
Jesus defends children's praise by appealing to Scripture (Ps 8:2), showing their acclaim fulfills God's word
The irony: children recognize Messiah; religious experts reject him. This fulfills Matt 11:25 (revealed to babes, hidden from wise)
The healings validate Jesus's authority. He has right to cleanse temple because God's power works through him

common_misinterpretations.error: This passage shows children's innocent worship is beautiful but theologically empty
common_misinterpretations.correction: The children's acclamation is theologically precise: 'Hosanna to Son of David' is explicit messianic claim. They recognize what chief priests refuse—Jesus is Davidic Messiah bringing salvation. Their praise fulfills Scripture (Ps 8:2, 118:25-26). This isn't cute innocence but spiritual insight. Jesus doesn't correct their theology but affirms it, defending it with Scripture against the 'experts.' The reversal is complete: children understand truth while trained theologians remain blind.
common_misinterpretations.scholars: R.T. France emphasizes children's praise is scripturally validated messianic acclamation. Craig Keener notes the leaders' indignation proves they understood the theological import—this wasn't harmless praise but serious claim. The passage illustrates kingdom reversal: 'God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise' (1 Cor 1:27).

common_misinterpretations.error: Jesus heals in temple as mere publicity stunt or opportunistic moment
common_misinterpretations.correction: The healing of blind and lame in temple is theologically loaded. These groups were excluded from full temple participation (2 Sam 5:8, rabbinic tradition). By healing them there, Jesus demonstrates the kingdom includes those the religious system excluded. This follows logically from the cleansing: first Jesus removes exploitative commerce, then he fills temple with marginalized people receiving healing. The temple becomes what God intended—house of prayer for all, place of mercy and inclusion, not exclusion and exploitation.
common_misinterpretations.scholars: Ulrich Luz notes the healings fulfill Isaiah 35:5-6 and reverse exclusionary practices. N.T. Wright sees this as enacting the new covenant community: barriers are removed, the excluded are welcomed. Dale Allison emphasizes the prophetic symbolism: Jesus reconfigures temple worship around mercy and inclusion.

overall_scholarly_interpretation.summary: Jesus's temple cleansing is prophetic sign-act judging corrupt temple leadership and foreshadowing temple's destruction. By driving out exploitative merchants, he reclaims the Court of the Gentiles for prayer, fulfilling Isaiah 56:7's vision. Quoting Jeremiah 7:11, he accuses leaders of using temple as hideout for their economic exploitation of pilgrims. After cleansing, he heals the blind and lame—groups excluded from full temple worship—demonstrating the kingdom's inclusivity. When children acclaim him as Messiah ('Hosanna to Son of David'), indignant leaders demand he stop them. Jesus defends the children by quoting Psalm 8:2, affirming God ordains praise from babes while learned experts reject truth. The cleansing accelerates the leaders' plot to kill Jesus (Mark 11:18).
major_themes: Prophetic judgment on corrupt temple system—commercial exploitation and Gentile exclusion
Jesus's authority to cleanse temple validated by healing miracles (Isaiah 35:5-6 fulfilled)
Reversal of religious exclusion: blind, lame, children welcomed; leaders indignant
Temple as 'house of prayer for all nations' vs 'den of robbers' (refuge for exploiters)
Children recognize Messiah; religious experts remain blind—wisdom revealed to babes (Matt 11:25)
Zeal for God's house consumes Jesus, leading to his death (Ps 69:9)
Foreshadowing temple's obsolescence—Jesus is the true temple (John 2:19-21)
historical_context: Court of Gentiles was outermost court, only place non-Jews could worship
Annas family (high priests) controlled temple market monopoly, exploiting pilgrims with inflated prices
Tyrian shekels required for temple tax due to silver purity; money changers charged extortionate rates
Animal sales necessary (pilgrims from distant lands couldn't bring sacrifices) but had become exploitative
Jesus's action directly challenged economic and political power of chief priests
This event accelerated plot to kill Jesus—he threatened both religious authority and economic interests
Temple destroyed 70 CE by Romans, ending sacrificial system—Jesus's action prophetically enacted this judgment

application_debates.question: Does this passage justify Christians using violence or force in righteous anger?
application_debates.position_1: Yes—Jesus used physical force (whip, overturning tables), so Christians may use force against injustice
application_debates.position_2: No—this was unique prophetic sign-act by Jesus as Messiah, not normative Christian behavior. Jesus didn't harm people, only disrupted commerce. Christian ethic is non-violence (Matt 5:39, Rom 12:19)
application_debates.consensus: Most scholars see this as unique prophetic act, not license for vigilante justice. Jesus had unique messianic authority to judge temple. Christians are called to confront injustice but through non-violent means (word, civil disobedience, systemic change). The zeal is commendable; the method was Jesus's unique prerogative.

application_debates.question: Does Jesus condemn all commerce or money in religious contexts?
application_debates.position_1: Yes—Jesus opposes mixing money and faith. Churches shouldn't handle money or charge for services
application_debates.position_2: No—Jesus condemns exploitation and Gentile exclusion, not necessary infrastructure. Temple tax required currency exchange. The issue is corruption, not finance per se
application_debates.consensus: Scholarly consensus favors position 2. Jesus doesn't reject temple tax or sacrificial system (he paid temple tax—Matt 17:24-27). The issue is exploitative monopoly controlled by corrupt priests and prevention of Gentile worship. Legitimate religious administration requires resources; exploitation of worshipers violates justice.

why_past_interpretations_were_incorrect.error: Jesus opposed temple worship and Jewish law
why_past_interpretations_were_incorrect.why_wrong: This anti-Jewish reading misses that Jesus's action affirms temple's purpose ('house of prayer') while judging its corruption. He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah—deeply Jewish prophetic critique. Jesus paid temple tax (Matt 17:24-27) and taught in temple regularly. The cleansing is prophetic call to reform, not rejection of Judaism.
why_past_interpretations_were_incorrect.correction: Modern scholarship (especially post-Holocaust) recognizes Jesus operated within Judaism as reformer, not founder of new religion. E.P. Sanders emphasizes Jesus's conflict was with temple leadership, not Judaism itself. The action is prophetic critique in tradition of Jeremiah and Malachi, not anti-Jewish polemic.

why_past_interpretations_were_incorrect.error: 'Den of robbers' means the temple had become site of theft/robbery
why_past_interpretations_were_incorrect.why_wrong: This misses Jeremiah 7:11's meaning. A 'den' is where robbers hide after crime, not where they rob. Jeremiah's point: people sin all week, then retreat to temple for false security. Jesus accuses leaders of exploiting pilgrims economically while hiding behind religious legitimacy.
why_past_interpretations_were_incorrect.correction: Understanding Jeremiah 7 context is crucial. God rejects worship disconnected from justice. The temple system had become tool of oppression—leaders extract wealth from poor in God's name, then claim temple's sanctity as cover. Jesus exposes hypocrisy: they're using religion to rob people, not worshiping God authentically.

conclusion_summary: The Temple Cleansing is prophetic theater—a dramatic sign-act enacting God's judgment on corrupt religious leadership. Jesus drives out merchants and money changers who have turned the Court of the Gentiles (meant for non-Jewish worship) into an exploitative marketplace. Quoting Isaiah 56:7, he reclaims temple as 'house of prayer for all nations.' Quoting Jeremiah 7:11, he accuses leaders of using temple as hideout ('den of robbers') after economically exploiting pilgrims. After cleansing, Jesus heals the blind and lame—those excluded from full temple participation—demonstrating the kingdom's radical inclusion. Children acclaim him as 'Son of David' (Messiah), but religious leaders are indignant. Jesus defends the children by citing Psalm 8:2, affirming God uses 'babes' to perfect praise while learned experts remain blind. This action directly challenges the economic and religious authority of chief priests, accelerating their plot to kill Jesus. The cleansing foreshadows temple's destruction (70 CE) and points to Jesus as the true temple—the place where God dwells and people meet God.
